attributes.grant-summary: A universal platform for DNA backbone functionalisation. DNA modification for biotechnology and nanoscience is hindered by expensive, time-consuming and highly specialised chemistry. This project will develop a platform for the universal attachment of diverse and functional building blocks to single-stranded DNA, editing the nucleic acid backbone rather than the nucleobases. This method will be cheaper, simpler and faster than existing solution- or solid-state technologies. Expected outcomes are the streamlined synthesis of functionalised DNA strands for biomaterials, sensing, and nanotechnology; accelerated biotechnology research through the eased accessibility of modified DNA; and the democratisation of functional DNA structures for nanomanufacturing, materials, and bioscience sectors.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
This Fellowship will develop chemistry for the universal attachment of functional molecules to the DNA backbone, transforming the use of nucleic acids in biotechnology, sensing, and advanced materials. Current modification technologies rely on expensive, bespoke chemistries that limit access and slow innovation. This Fellowship will develop a new platform that provides simple, low-cost, and scalable routes to produce functionalised DNA strands quickly using standard laboratory infrastructure.

By enabling affordable, high-throughput DNA modification, this Fellowship will accelerate the development of smart diagnostics, sensors, and nanotechnologies, supporting Australia’s sovereign capacity in nucleic acid manufacturing, synthetic biology, and bioengineering. The Fellowship outcomes align directly with Australia’s National Science and Research Priorities (2024) in 'Building a Secure and Resilient Nation' and with the List of Critical Technologies in the National Interest (2023) under 'Advanced Manufacturing' and 'Biotechnology'.

The global nucleic acid synthesis market was valued at US$11 billion in 2025 and is projected to be $25 billion by 2030. This Fellowship will harness this growth to position Australia as a global leader in DNA chemistry. It will build new international and industry partnerships, train a skilled workforce in cutting-edge DNA functionalisation, and strengthen the nation’s biotechnology capacity, innovation pipeline, and economic competitiveness.

attributes.grant-summary: New geometry-driven statistics tools tuned to reveal vital geological clues. The project aims to develop new statistical methods to uncover hidden geological signals by extracting the most relevant information from noisy geoscience databases with complex structures. This project is at the interface between mathematical statistics, geophysics and geochemistry and it will integrate cutting-edge concepts from all three fields to generate new knowledge. These advances in knowledge will lead to an enhanced ability to discriminate natural events such as earthquakes from clandestine nuclear tests, and by doing so support Australia’s commitment to the comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty. Other outcomes are improved methods for identifying previously undetected critical mineral deposits which is a national priority.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop new software specifically designed to analyse complex geoscience databases, focusing on two key issues: better detection of nuclear tests and critical mineral deposits. Outcomes will provide significant economic, environmental and social benefits by improving our security against nuclear threats and ensuring Australia’s supply of critical strategic minerals. The 1996 Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty endorsed by Australia theoretically put a stop to all nuclear bomb testing worldwide. However, the 3 major nuclear powers (China, Russia and the USA) appear to be preparing for nuclear testing again. In this context, it is essential for Australia to rapidly monitor nuclear testing. This project will develop improved explosion monitoring software, capable of detecting covert, underground nuclear tests. Australia’s 2024-25 Federal budget included $566 million for Geoscience Australia (GA) to map the nation's critical minerals, needed for the clean energy transition to a net zero future. This project will deliver the necessary software to analyse GA’s geochemistry data, Australia’s magnetic field records and other databases.  Better analysis of these databases will facilitate critical mineral discovery. The outcomes will be shared, disseminated and adopted through an online repository of open-source R and Python tools, and promoted via collaboration with GA as well as national and international networks of users from research, government and industry.

attributes.grant-summary: Activating archived ancestral knowledge for Warlpiri women's ceremonies. This project aims to support the revitalisation of Warlpiri women's song traditions by uncovering how archival resources can be used to develop targeted action plans for intergenerational transmission of song knowledge and practices. In collaboration with Warlpiri women and Central Australian organisations, the project will investigate generational shifts to learning songs and develop methods and resources for their maintenance through an innovative and reproducible model for revitalisation of Indigenous song and dance practices. This should provide significant benefits in ensuring that this knowledge and these practices are maintained across generations as a vital part of Australia's unique national and cultural identity.
attributes.primary-field-of-research: 4501 - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Culture, Language and History
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures are critical to Australian national identity and it is imperative that these the ceremonial song traditions at the heart of culture are recognised and supported. For Warlpiri women living in communities across the Tanami desert region of Central Australia, the ceremonies that have been passed on to them through generations are vital to their cultural identity and well-being. Yet there is a concern amongst present day Warlpiri women for the cultural health of future generations as these songs are not being passed on to younger generations as effectively as they were in past eras. This project will address a key research gap in determining how archived materials can be used for revitalisation so that old songs, dances and designs can form active parts of vibrant contemporary ceremonies. It will answer new questions about contemporary song learning and collaborate with local archival, educational and community arts organisations to develop targeted strategies to enhance intergenerational transmission. Through development of a reproducible model for revitalisation of Indigenous song and dance traditions this project will extend to benefit similarly culturally vulnerable communities and will provide benefits to Australian society by ensuring Australian rich Indigenous cultural identity is kept strong and can inform cultural policy.

attributes.grant-summary: Death by Corporation: Criminal Law, Culture and Homicidal Corporations. Corporations kill on a scale that far exceeds those caused by individuals, yet prosecutions for corporate homicide are exceedingly rare. This project aims to challenge the failure to conceptualise corporate killings as unlawful homicides. By employing a transdisciplinary approach, the project will critically analyse legal and cultural conceptualisations of corporate killings to address the obstacles preventing the criminal liability of corporations. The intended outcome is to present a compelling argument of how corporations can and should be prosecuted for homicide, leading to significant legal, economic and social benefits by prohibiting and deterring corporate homicides specifically and corporate harms more broadly.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: In Australia and globally corporations kill with products and practices on a scale vastly exceeding homicides caused by individuals eg approximately 4,000 Australians die from asbestos related disease each year. Yet corporations are rarely, if ever, prosecuted for homicide. These deaths cause grief to victims and their families, and have long-term economic and social costs, as corporations often externalise harms, leaving individuals and governments to bear costs such as health care and environmental clean-ups. Given that homicide is a fundamental concept in criminal law, and how widespread these slayings are, criminal law should be applied, but it is as though we cannot even imagine it. This reflects a broader failure to imagine the corporation as criminal, shown in limited law scholarship on corporate deaths. In the absence of criminal law, corporations undertake a cost benefit analysis of harms, including death, normalising them as acceptable costs of business. In contrast, criminal law conveys that killing is prohibited and morally unacceptable. By examining corporate homicide through the lens of philosophies of wickedness and horror, this project provides a pragmatic, principled and imaginative framework justifying the prosecution of corporations for manslaughter or murder. Outcomes shared with law practitioners may lead to a greater ability to hold corporations responsible for wrongdoing and, by deterring harmful actions, a decrease in harms caused by corporations.

attributes.grant-summary: Breaking the Bacterial Barrier by Selective Membrane-Active Peptides. This project aims to develop new and efficient methods for the rapid molecular design of membrane-active peptides that can target specific bacterial membranes. These methods are expected to overcome the challenges of high costs of production, time-consuming synthesis, instability, and determining membrane activity, which have limited their development to date. This novel approach is expected to create peptides that target specific membranes in various bacteria. This should benefit Australian research and industry by establishing an efficient molecular design system that can be applied to peptide discovery for diverse purposes and by commercialising novel membrane-active peptides.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
Bacterial membranes provide a barrier between cell contents and their environment. The ability to specifically disrupt or penetrate these membranes has huge potential in industrial, research and health settings. For example membranes can be targeted for destruction, signalling, release of compounds of interest or to study membrane biophysics. Discovering membrane-active peptides remains challenging and time-consuming.
This project aims to develop novel technologies that enable the rapid and high throughput design of membrane-active peptides- small chains of amino acids that can specifically interact with membranes of various types. My Fellowship research will enable the future development of approaches to target bacteria of interest. This will have broad applications including food preservation, biofilm control, crop protection and veterinary health management. The resulting compounds and methods will provide benefits to Australia through their future commercialisation for anti-microbial use in agricultural, veterinary and human diseases. 
Findings will be communicated to target stakeholders through events such as the University Partner Showcase, the annual US Bio conference and advocacy groups such as AusBiotech to maximise translation and to seek new opportunities with non-academic partners. We will also disseminate our findings to the public via the media, utilising channels such as La Trobe media, Social media, team website, and podcasts.

attributes.grant-summary: Broad pH-Range Redox Flow Batteries with Sustainable Fluorine-Free Membrane. This project aims to develop highly ion-selective, sustainable fluorine-free membranes for redox flow batteries – an essential technology for large-scale renewable energy storage. By precisely tuning the membranes’ microstructure to create efficient ion pathways, the project will deliver robust, sustainable, durable, high-performance membranes compatible with both acidic and alkaline redox flow batteries. This work will provide deep insights into polymers design and synthesis, thereby guiding the future optimization of membranes for different redox flow batteries. This project will significantly promote Australia's leadership in green energy storage and manufacturing, supporting Australia’s commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop a super-duper membrane used to increase the lifespan and efficiency of a large-scale energy storage batteries to store electricity generated from renewable sources such as wind and solar power, to address Australia’s urgent need for sustainable, cost-effective, and environmentally responsible grid-scale energy storage solutions. The project aims to fill a critical research gap by developing cost-effective and high-performance fluorine-free alternative membranes that are scalable, durable, sustainable, and locally relevant. Economically, this research supports the local manufacturing of key materials for clean energy, reduces reliance on foreign imports for such materials, and creates jobs and wealth within high-tech industries. Environmentally, it eliminates hazardous fluorinated waste streams, enabling cleaner lifecycle management of large-scale batteries. Socially and commercially, reliable and affordable long-duration energy storage will strengthen renewable energy integration, reduce electricity costs, and support Australia’s transition toward net-zero emissions. A series of educational and outreach activities will be conducted including to disseminating research findings through curricula to graduate students, undergraduates, and even younger students; engaging in free lectures for communities and remote regions to publicize research outcomes; and sharing research summaries via short videos online to enhance dissemination effectiveness.

attributes.grant-summary: Tuning a Galactic Gravitational-Wave Detector using Pulsar Scintillation. This project aims to improve the detection of ultra-low-frequency gravitational waves by developing new models that link pulsar radio-wave scintillation to noise processes in the interstellar medium through hierarchical statistical inference. The project expects to generate new knowledge about how plasma in the interstellar medium affects pulsar signals, using innovative techniques that transform interstellar scattering from a source of noise into a calibration tool. Expected outcomes include advanced software for precision gravitational-wave detection and improved characterisation of the interstellar medium. This will enhance Australia’s leadership in radio astronomy and strengthen the scientific return from the Square Kilometre Array.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
Australia is investing heavily in the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest radio telescope, to explore the universe through radio waves and train the next generation of scientists and engineers. One barrier to its success is that signals from pulsars — rapidly rotating neutron stars used to detect low-frequency gravitational waves — are distorted as they pass through the interstellar medium. This project will overcome that problem by linking the twinkling, or "scintillation," of pulsar radio signals to the distortions that affect gravitational-wave analyses, through advanced hierarchical statistical models.

By transforming a source of interference into a source of precision, the project will strengthen Australia’s capacity to detect gravitational waves from merging supermassive black holes, a major scientific frontier. The same techniques will also improve understanding of the Sun’s plasma environment, benefiting national space-weather forecasting that protects communications, power grids, and satellite systems.

To maximise public benefit, all software and results will be openly released, accompanied by public talks, workshops, and accessible science articles. Collaborations with international radio telescopes will showcase Australia’s leadership in gravitational-wave astronomy and solar plasma physics, ensuring that national investment in the SKA delivers lasting scientific, technological, workforce, and cultural returns for Australia and its partners.

attributes.grant-summary: Costs and unexpected benefits of sickness and motivational presenteeism. 58% of employees in Australian organisations are at work, but not working at maximum capacity due to ill-health or low motivation – otherwise known as presenteeism. This project aims to explore why this is the case, particularly among women and racially diverse workers, many of whom are overqualified. Utilising high-fidelity experimental and field studies, this project examines why: (a) presenteeism increases ostracism of minority employees, but (b) decreases loneliness - a growing public health concern; and (c) how organisations can minimise costs and maximise benefits of presenteeism. The benefits are actionable steps for organisations to prevent sickness and promote health among all employees, despite overqualification or demographics.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Nearly 60% of Australians engage in presenteeism - they go to work but not working at maximum capacity due to ill-health or low motivation. Presenteeism costs Australian economy $6.1 billion a year due to lost productivity. Yet employees, particularly women and racially diverse workers may have valid reasons for engaging in presenteeism such as job security concerns, reluctance to overburden peers, or avoiding feeling lonely at home. In addition to sickness presenteeism, 1 in 5 Australians engage in hidden presenteeism when they come to work with anxiety and depression, but do not disclose these issues out of stigma fears. This research examines how organisations can minimise presenteeism whilst treating their minority employees equitably. The economic benefits include the increased knowledge about how organisations can prevent sickness and hence minimise costs. The social benefits include (a) knowledge about how to promote health and wellbeing, when employees feel psychologically safe to disclose their sickness and hence avoid presenteeism; and (b) the discovery of unexpected benefits – decreased loneliness among those with mental ill-health. Societal benefits are: (a) considering specific types of sick leave that cover a wider range of impairing conditions; and (b) implementing disclosure and anti-stigma training to increase awareness of presenteeism cost. The outcomes will be disseminated to industry via practitioner-oriented publications, media interactions, and podcasts.

attributes.grant-summary: Understanding young people’s deliberations about what knowledge to trust. This project aims to investigate how secondary school students decide what knowledge to trust and the best policies and practices to support them. It expects to advance new understanding of the role of schooling in young people’s deliberations on trustworthy knowledge amid rising public debate and uncertainty. Expected outcomes include enhanced capacity to develop effective school policies and practices through the application of innovative participatory methods with young people, policy and curricula analysis, and research with stakeholders and teachers. Significant benefits should include improved outcomes, professional development, and better community understanding of the social and cultural factors in deciding what knowledge to trust.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Young people in Australia face significant challenges in deciding what knowledge to trust, and their schools are struggling to support them. Misinformation, rapid changes in digital information, artificial intelligence, and intensifying social and cultural divisions are all contributing to rising public uncertainty about what knowledge is trustworthy. Yet, we know very little about how young people decide themselves what knowledge is reliable, the social and cultural factors that shape these decisions, or how schools and teachers can best assist them. This project addresses this gap through a multi-pronged research agenda, involving innovative participatory research with secondary school students, policy and curriculum analysis, and research with teachers, policymakers, and community members. This will produce much-needed evidence and guidance for effective schooling policies and practices. Public benefit is also ensured through major public-facing outputs, including a Policy Brief and Policy Paper to inform best policy development. In addition, a Professional Resource Package will enable teacher professional development and publicly available Research Vignettes will provide crucial community insight into young people’s deliberations. Project findings will better equip Australian communities, schools, and families to navigate fast changing knowledge practices and support the next generation grapple with new complexities in determining trustworthy knowledge.

attributes.grant-summary:
Real-time mass spectrometry for elucidating marine aerosol processes. This project aims to provide fundamental process-level understanding of atmospheric aerosol processes over the Southern Ocean, a region critical to the Australian and global climate and where climate models perform poorly. Comprehensive observations during a Southern Ocean voyage and intense laboratory experiments will enhance our knowledge of aerosols and their  influence on cloud formation in that region and provide much needed data for improving global climate models. Expected outcomes include more accurate seasonal and latitudinal representations of Southern Ocean aerosol populations, properties and sources. The main benefit
includes improved weather forecasting and future climate projections for Australia and the Southern Hemisphere.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Atmospheric processes over the Southern Ocean have a profound influence on regional and global climate. This is a part of the world where global climate models perform particularly poorly. This project is addressing the greatest source of uncertainty in climate models – atmospheric aerosols and how they influence cloud formation. Observational data for the Southern Ocean are scarce and this project is a unique opportunity to gather much-needed observations in this region. By using state-of-the-art instrumentation during a 60 days long voyage on the Australian research vessel Investigator and targeted laboratory measurements, the project will enhance our knowledge of the aerosol formation and transformation processes over the Southern Ocean and the role of ocean microorganisms on aerosol properties and populations in the Southern Ocean atmosphere. The new knowledge gained in the project will contribute to improving and strengthening the predictive skill of global climate models. Australia is heavily exposed to weather and climate risk, impacting the safety and well-being of Australians and the productivity of diverse industries. Improved climate projections from models that better represent the Southern Ocean atmospheric processes will inform robust strategies for climate change adaptation, mitigation, and resilience, and better prepare Australia for the challenges of a variable and changing climate.

attributes.grant-summary: Rethinking Comparative Ethics through Early Modern Sino-Western Encounters. This project aims to uncover the forgotten origins of Sino-Western comparative ethics and assess its significance for rethinking the field today. By recovering neglected texts in Chinese, Latin and Italian, the project expects to generate significant new knowledge about how early modern Jesuits and their Chinese interlocutors pursued ethical dialogue between scholastic-Aristotelian and neo-Confucian thought. The expected outcome is a new philologically and historically rooted approach to comparative ethics that foregrounds commentarial traditions and normative values. Benefits include the first history of how Sino-Western comparative ethics emerged and new insights into making comparative ethics more responsive to lived moral experience.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: This project reconstructs for the first time the methodologies developed by early modern Jesuit missionaries in China and their Chinese interlocutors to compare scholastic-Aristotelian and neo-Confucian ethics and assesses their enduring relevance for comparative ethics today. Whereas contemporary Sino-Western comparative ethics often centres on ancient texts, these early modern methodologies highlighted how ethical traditions were received, adapted and valued within their respective communities. By redirecting the discipline’s focus from abstract concepts to the normative values informing community practices, the project will make Sino-Western comparative ethics more responsive to real-world moral experience and thus more relevant to cross-cultural ethical dialogue in multicultural societies like Australia. The translation and analysis of key Latin and Chinese-language sources will open up these materials for scholarly inquiry and to the wider Australian public. The organisation of a major public facing event and targeted media engagement will ensure that research outcomes reach beyond academia, enriching community understanding of the importance of comparative ethics. Finally, the project will consolidate Australia's global leadership in research on Sino-Western intercultural research and foster the next generation of Australian researchers in this rapidly expanding field.

attributes.grant-summary: Nonlinear Ultrasonics: Transforming Diagnosis & Prognosis of Infrastructure. This Fellowship aims to develop new technology and frameworks for structural damage diagnosis and prognosis – leveraging nonlinear ultrasonics – to address substantial limitations in existing safety inspection and forecasting systems for engineering structures. The project will establish important knowledge across nondestructive testing and structural health monitoring, with innovations spanning nonlinear feature extraction, reference-free diagnostics, and the first system-level structural safety prognostics methodology for diverse infrastructure. Outcomes include key improvements for infrastructure reliability and operational safety, and reductions in the unsustainable financial burden of current maintenance and management practice.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
Early detection of damage and accurate prediction of remaining service life are critical to the integrity, safety, and effective management of high-value infrastructure assets. Existing techniques, however, are largely insensitive to incipient damage and often provide diagnostic information that is insufficient to support reliable decisions on maintenance/rehabilitation/repair and infrastructure life prediction.

This project will advance the scientific foundations of nonlinear ultrasonics to deliver a robust technology for structural health monitoring. Exploiting the physical nonlinearities induced by emerging structural damage (e.g., fatigue cracks, debonding), developing novel diagnostics, and designing system-level safety prognostics, the research will enable accurate assessment and life prediction. This would help transform conventional schedule-based inspection approaches to proactive, data-driven, condition-based inspection.

Significant economic and social benefits for Australia include lowered infrastructure maintenance costs, enhanced safety, minimised disruptions/downtime, and strengthened sovereign capability across key and emerging industry sectors. The research will expand Australia’s leading expertise in non-destructive inspection – a global market projected to exceed US$18 billion by 2031. Findings will be communicated to a range of government agencies and research organisations, including via workshops, and more broadly through traditional and social media.

attributes.current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
attributes.announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
attributes.grant-summary: Solar driven chalcogenide tandems for unassisted green ammonia production. This project aims to develop an all-chalcogenide tandem photoelectrochemical system for unassisted, solar-driven green ammonia production. By integrating two stable and low-cost chalcogenide semiconductors into a single tandem device, the research will enable efficient ammonia conversion without external power. Expected outcomes include new understanding of carrier transport, interface engineering, and reaction selectivity in solar chemical systems, and practical design principles for stable, high-efficiency devices. This will enable a transformative route for green hydrogen storage and transport, while offering additional pathways for valuable products, advancing Australia’s leadership in clean energy innovation and net-zero transition.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
This project will advance Australia’s leadership in renewable energy by developing a new solar technology that directly converts sunlight into clean ammonia, a vital energy carrier for the nation’s hydrogen economy. Ammonia is central to the Australian Government’s National Hydrogen Strategy and Future Made in Australia Act, as it enables safe and cost-effective storage and export of green hydrogen. The project’s innovative all-chalcogenide tandem photoelectrochemical system will produce green ammonia directly from nitrate-rich agricultural runoff and industrial effluents using only sunlight and water, offering a low-cost, carbon-free alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process.
This research aligns with the National Science and Research Priorities, particularly “Transitioning to a net zero future” and “Protecting and restoring Australia’s environment”. It will deliver environmental benefits by reducing industrial pollution, economic benefits through scalable green ammonia production, and social benefits by supporting regional industries and agricultural sustainability. The outcomes will strengthen Australia’s renewable manufacturing capability, expand expertise in advanced materials, and train the next generation of researchers in solar-fuel technologies. Collectively, this project will position Australia as a trusted global supplier of green hydrogen and ammonia, accelerating the nation’s transition toward a clean, secure and sustainable energy future.

attributes.grant-summary: Reforming Corporate Ethics: A Programmatic Agenda . This Fellowship aims to build a new ethical framework for business corporations, in light of recent Australian corporate scandals. It expects to generate a rigorous, philosophically grounded framework that reimagines what business corporations are and what they are for, using an innovative methodology that engages business ethics advisors and policymakers in ethical dialogue. Expected outcomes include new ethical principles to guide corporate governance and regulation, focused on the energy, care, and banking sectors. By reconceiving how business corporations can be contributors to wellbeing, the Fellowship's benefits will include a positive transformation in how we understand and conceptualise ethics in business.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Must business corporations advance the common good, or should they be permitted to narrowly pursue private profit? This question has gained urgency following recent controversies, including fossil fuel expansions, egregious allegations in for-profit childcare, and regulatory action against major banks. We have no robust ethical framework for understanding what business corporations are for, or what ethical responsibilities they can—and should—bear. To address this gap, Australia needs to reform the ethical orientation of business corporations. This Fellowship will develop a rigorous and philosophically-grounded framework that reimagines what business corporations are and what they are for, using a collaborative methodology in which business ethics advisors and policymakers are engaged in dialogue. Focusing on the energy, care, and banking sectors, the project will develop new guidelines for corporate governance and regulation. This will benefit Australians by supporting principled regulation and enabling corporations to contribute positively to climate, care, and finance. The project will create impact beyond academia by producing a policy-oriented white paper, delivering tailored workshops for business leaders, and engaging the broader public through podcasts and media commentaries. These activities will translate the project’s insights into accessible and practical guidance, shaping public debate and fostering a more ethics-driven business sector in Australia.

attributes.grant-summary: Preventing Sexualised Deepfake Abuse with Evidence-Based Interventions. Emerging AI technologies are fuelling sexual violence and outpacing prevention measures. This Fellowship will investigate the factors driving sexualised deepfake abuse (the non-consensual creation/sharing of AI-generated sexual content) and produce new knowledge on the social, digital and cultural environments enabling it. It aims to advance understanding of AI misuse and identify effective preventions using interdisciplinary social, technological and legal approaches. Expected outcomes include improved policy, reduced harms, and building Australia’s leadership in ethical AI. Expected benefits include protecting Australians with evidence-based policies and practice to prevent sexualised deepfake abuse and future AI-facilitated harms.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
It takes one clear image, 25 minutes and no cost to create a realistic, but entirely fake pornographic video with AI. In the past 18 months, reports of AI-generated sexual content of Australians under 18 years more than doubled; 80% of victims were women. Laws are an important step towards prevention, but criminalisation alone cannot stop AI-generated sexual violence. Prevention requires research, education, technology and collaboration, alongside comprehensive legal action.

This project addresses the urgent problem of sexualised deepfake abuse–the non-consensual creation, sharing or threat to share AI-generated sexual content. By integrating new data, theory and analysis, this project investigates the technologies driving this abuse and the social and digital environments that enable it. The project will produce significant benefits that protect Australians from emerging AI-facilitated harms, support safer digital environments and guide responsible AI use. It will deliver practical strategies for governments, NGOs, digital platforms and bystanders (friends, peers, families) to prevent the misuse of AI, providing social and economic benefits. 

To maximise impact, findings will be communicated through accessible reports, workshops, policy briefings and collaborations with platforms and diverse community groups, ensuring the evidence informs real-world practice, strengthens Australia’s leadership in the ethical use of AI and drives global understandings of AI-harm prevention.

attributes.grant-summary: Soil microbiomes for repairing climate-resilient ecosystems. This project aims to strengthen the climate resilience of ecosystems under repair. Soil microbiomes – diverse communities of bacteria, fungi and other microbes that form the foundation of soil health – underpin ecosystem climate resilience but remain largely overlooked in restoration practice. By revealing how soil microbiomes support native plants under climate stress, developing effective ways to introduce them in real-world settings, and building new international networks for translation and training, this research will transform how we restore ecosystems in crisis. These advances will deliver new ways to repair biodiversity and support national goals for nature conservation, healthy soils, climate adaptation and sustainable growth.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
This Fellowship will establish Australia’s first research program on soil microbiomes to support ecosystem repair and climate resilience. While healthy soil is essential to climate resilience, the microbial life that underpins it remains poorly integrated into restoration science, practice and policy. This project will investigate how soil microbiomes improve plant fitness under climate stress, identify scalable delivery methods, and validate outcomes in real-world contexts across diverse Australian landscapes. 
It will also produce best-practice guidelines, decision-support tools, and training resources for land managers and policymakers. Expected benefits include faster ecosystem recovery, reduced replanting costs, improved mine-site rehabilitation, and new opportunities in biodiversity and carbon markets. These outcomes will align with national priorities on protecting and restoring Australia’s environment, climate change, soil health, and sustainable economic growth. 
To promote uptake beyond academia, the project will be co-produced with government, NGO, and industry partners. Results will be shared through open data platforms, practitioner guidelines, and targeted training through workshops, policy briefings and demonstration filed days to maximise translation and adoption of findings. This will help catalyse a new microbiome restoration sector, build national capacity and skills, and create jobs across Australia.

attributes.grant-summary: Enabling resilience to climate extremes in future plant communities. Temperature and humidity determine limits to plant life in complex environments, yet we currently lack the ability to predict how these limits will affect communities as extreme climatic events intensify. This project aims to use innovative experiments and unified models to evaluate exposure and sensitivity of plant communities to heat and drying. Expected outcomes include fundamental knowledge of limits and plant strategies to mitigate and tolerate extremes, and enhanced conservation capacity via new software integrating plant physiology with microclimate ecology. Expected benefits included enhanced risk evaluation that underpins adaptation strategies in natural and urban ecosystems to minimise effects of a hotter, less predictable future.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Extreme climatic events like heatwaves and hot droughts can severely impact ecosystems, agriculture and urban environments. Life-threatening heatwaves are becoming more severe and frequent. We urgently need to understand how plants communities can cope with extremes to assess true vulnerability and develop strategies to safeguard the vital services they provide to nature and society. This project aims to resolve this critical gap by pairing experiments and models to understand and predict limits to plant function during extremes and their capacity to recover. Australia will benefit from this project by building capacity to forecast climate impacts on plants broadly. Australia's environments are valued at $80B for climate regulation, water supply and grazing, while healthy biodiverse ecosystems are immensely valuable for culture and tourism. Most of Australia’s population lives in urban environments where plants provide essential cooling, shading and air quality services that support health and liveability. While this project centres on natural and urban vegetation, it applies to Australian commercial and economic industries that rely on continued plant resilience: forestry ($11B), agricultural crops ($28B) and horticulture ($17B). Collaborations with botanic gardens and conservation managers will support practical adaptation strategies while public engagement through workshops and citizen science will ensure broad understanding and inspire hope for a greener, cooler future.

attributes.grant-summary: Nanoscale restructuring of porous carbons for efficient energy storage. The project aims to develop a new class of flexible porous carbons for energy storage using a novel restructuring strategy based on organic solvents. Current porous carbons lack flexibility, limiting their usability where features such as wettability, conductivity, and graphitization are essential. The project will study how solvent-induced restructuring enables flexibility using advanced computational and spectroscopic studies, and intriguing preliminary results strengthen the project. Expected outcomes include low-cost and scalable electrode materials for energy storage. The work will generate new knowledge, benefit Australia’s transition to net-zero emissions targets, strengthen collaboration, and train emerging materials scientists.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s transition to renewable energy is crucial for achieving net-zero emissions and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. However, the widespread adoption of renewables in the energy sector is hindered mainly by the lack of safe, affordable, and high-performance energy storage materials. Traditional carbon materials used for energy storage are amorphous, rigid, and hydrophobic, limiting their ability to store energy efficiently. This fellowship aims to address this challenge by developing a new type of carbon-based energy storage material from waste biomass like agricultural residues using a novel technique that employs organic solvents to reshape the carbon structure, making it more flexible and better at conducting electricity. This increased flexibility will improve its ability to absorb and move ions. The research will also explore how the solvent works at a microscopic level to relax the internal stress in the carbon, helping it take on the desired structure. This approach not only improves energy storage but also supports environmental sustainability by recycling waste and contributing to the circular economy. The outcomes will enable the development of low-cost energy storage materials crucial for energy generation and storage industries, thereby strengthening Australia's energy security. To ensure broader impact, public engagement, and industrial partnerships will be stimulated through collaboration with clean tech businesses and social enterprise collaborations.

attributes.grant-summary: Flexible Inorganic Thermoelectrics for Wearable Power Generation. Wearable thermoelectrics can directly convert body heat into electricity, providing a sustainable solution for powering wearable electronics. However, their limited performance and durability currently restrict practical use. This project will develop new low-cost, environmentally friendly materials for flexible thermoelectric devices based on magnesium-based films. Using advanced synthesis and mechanisms, it aims to achieve high energy-conversion efficiency and mechanical flexibility for durable, self-charging electronics. The outcomes include improved materials and device designs, scalable fabrication methods, and training for young researchers, strengthening Australia’s leadership in sustainable energy and advanced materials innovation.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to develop next-generation magnesium-based flexible thermoelectric thin films and devices that efficiently harvest body heat to power wearable electronics. Current flexible thermoelectric technologies are constrained by low output power, poor mechanical stability, and high cost. By integrating advanced band/interface engineering, scalable thin-film fabrication, and device design, this research will address a critical gap in delivering high-performance, low-cost, and eco-friendly flexible thermoelectrics for sustainable energy conversion in Australia.
The outcomes will support Australia’s economic and environmental priorities by enabling maintenance-free, self-powered electronics, reducing dependence on batteries and fossil fuels. This technology can be applied in healthcare (e.g., medical sensors, pacemakers), defence wearables, smart textiles, and energy recovery systems, driving innovation in advanced manufacturing. Environmentally, it contributes to decarbonisation by converting waste heat into clean electricity, aligning with national net-zero targets.
To maximise impact beyond academia, outcomes will be translated through industry partnerships, IP protection, and commercial pathways. Engagement with the ARC Research Hub in Zero-emission Power Generation, industry, and government, along with public demonstrations and outreach via national and international platforms, will promote a broad understanding, adoption, and long-term benefits for Australians.

attributes.grant-summary: Speed Matters: Overcoming Slow Convergence in Mathematical Optimisation. This project will develop the mathematical foundations needed for improving the performance of iterative methods from optimisation without requiring additional computational power. Although accelerated optimisation algorithms are now central to machine learning, the underlying mechanisms behind their effectiveness remain poorly understood. Building on recent breakthroughs in the field, this project expects to develop new mechanisms for improving performance in optimisation and take key steps towards a general mathematical theory of acceleration. The project is expected to provide significant benefits in large-scale machine learning where computational performance directly translates into energy consumption.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Large-scale artificial intelligence is having a transformative effect on society, enabling innovations such as self-driving cars, early disease detection and next-generation climate models. However, this excitement is being tempered by concerns in the unsustainable energy demands of these technologies and their associated environmental impact. Underlying many of the energy-intensive components in these technologies are tools from the field of mathematical optimisation. This project will advance research in mathematical optimisation to develop improved versions of these tools, which perform the same tasks with significantly less energy usage. The research will position Australia as a world leader in optimisation technologies as well as reduce environment impact in its applications such as artificial intelligence. Outcomes from this project will be communicated through academic journals, public lectures and research-based news platforms.

attributes.grant-summary: Soft Robotic Atrioventricular Model to Unravel Motion-Haemodynamic Coupling. This fellowship develops an assistive soft robotic simulator to unveil new understanding on how motion, fluidic pressure and flow drive the heart. It gives fundamental insights into heart's mechanical and fluidic mechanisms that are inaccessible from current simulator or animal models. By recreating these complex processes, it unlocks core principles and shows how prosthetic and assistive device interact and alter heart performance. Outcomes include new method to fabricate and control soft robotic organs, atlas for better cardiac & assistive device design, new benchmarks & testbeds for research and skill training. It will also foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, enhance Australia’s research, education, benefit consumers and healthcare.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: A cardiac simulator is a physical platform that reproduces the heart motion, pressure, and flow for engineering evaluation, teaching, and research. It is needed because animals are typically healthy and cannot replicate specific heart conditions, while current simulators fail to capture heart’s complex 3D motions and flow. The global cardiac-device market is valued at US$60B, yet many prototypes stall before translation due to inadequate, non-reproducible testing. This project will create the first tunable soft-robotic heart as an ethical, repeatable testbed that reduces reliance on animals and enables controlled studies beyond current rigs. Outcomes include new methods for manufacturing soft robotic components, sensing and control, and open datasets, protocols and benchmarks that raise national standards. The work aligns with Australian priorities in robotics, sensing, AI and high-value manufacturing, and with global trends emphasising non-animal methods (e.g., NIH), Australia’s 3Rs initiative to replace or reduce animal studies. It will build sovereign capability to design, fabricate and validate complex bio-inspired systems domestically, reducing costly offshore testing and strengthening med-tech supply chains. The project will train a cross-disciplinary workforce and produce interoperable tools for future device testing, education and skills development. Anticipated benefits include lower R&D costs, fewer animal studies, improved export readiness, and new high-value jobs.

attributes.grant-summary: Atomically sharp interfaces for in-material retina-like motion perception. This project aims to understand the peculiar light-matter interactions in defect-rich optically-active materials and their hybrids. By engineering stacked heterostructures, this project will create materials with bipolar and persistent photoelectrical properties, not possible using current solid state electronics. This will result in new optoelectronic materials that mimic the analog motion perception of retinal bipolar cells. Expected outcomes include new knowledge of how intrinsic defects in extremely thin semiconductor materials can be used to achieve in-material visual scene detection, storage and processing. This should provide benefits in miniaturised materials for autonomous sensing systems in size and power-constrained environments.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement: Miniaturised devices capable of perceiving motion in images, similar to human vision, are set to transform future computing and autonomous sensing by eliminating the need for separate, power-hungry components while enabling real-time decision-making based on sensor data. This transition is essential to reduce Australia's growing energy footprint while enabling next-generation technologies for transport, health, defence, and smart environments. Inspired by the sophisticated and energy-efficient nature of human vision, and specifically the role of analog motion perception in retinal cells, this project addresses foundational gaps in realising such hardware. Leveraging advances in materials engineering and optical science, the research aligns with Australia's strategic interest in critical technologies, fostering sovereign capability in intelligent sensors and miniaturised imaging platforms. Anticipated outcomes include new economic, social, and employment opportunities, empowering Australia to lead in areas such as autonomous vehicles, environmental monitoring, portable health systems, space and agricultural sensing, and self-guided manufacturing. The project supports national priorities advancing Australia's competitiveness and security in an evolving global landscape. Outcomes will be promoted through industry partnerships, targeted demonstrations to end-users, open-access publications, patent protection, and engagement with government to accelerate commercial translation.

attributes.grant-summary: Developing novel time use tools to support ageing in place. This project aims to develop and validate an AI-enhanced, open-access digital tool, the MARCA+, that will transform time-use research and support cognitive and brain ageing. Aim 1 will identify the time-use patterns most strongly associated with cognitive function and brain outcomes using novel compositional longitudinal modelling. These insights will inform Aims 2 and 3, which will co-design and validate the MARCA+ tool to enable automated recall and classification of daily activity context. Co-designed with key stakeholders, the tool will enable scalable, context-rich data collection at a population level for the first time.
attributes.national-interest-test-statement:
Understanding how daily activity patterns influence cognitive and brain ageing is critical to addressing the challenges of Australia’s ageing population. Over the next 15 years, the proportion of Australians aged over 65 is projected to increase from 16% to 20%, amplifying the need for scalable, evidence-based strategies that enable population-level surveillance of lifestyle behaviours. This project will apply artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to advance time-use research by co-designing a scalable, open-access tool that captures rich time-use data, including screen time, cognitive load and activity context. The tool will link with wearable data, and other available health data from mobile phones, enabling large-scale, longitudinal research into the behavioural determinants of successful ageing.
The project will deliver economic and social benefits by reducing the reliance on residential aged care, empowering older Australians to remain independent and engaged. Creating a tool suitable for older Australian’s will scale easily for younger populations, leading to commercial opportunities in Australia’s growing digital health sector. The project will also provide advanced training for Early Career Researchers and PhD students in AI, machine learning and co-design, strengthening Australia’s research capacity and positioning it as a global leader in digital innovations for successful ageing.
